summary.text:
A district council carrying £175.4m of capital financing requirement against £82.7m of actual external borrowing. The £92.7m gap is funded from its own cash — the council's balance sheet forecast calls it internal borrowing — and that cash is running down: usable reserves fall from £126.5m to £112.9m across the year and treasury investments from £50.2m to £35.8m. Internal borrowing is only free while there is something to borrow from.

The 2026/27 capital programme is £102.7m (£58.4m HRA, £44.3m General Fund) with £30.6m of new borrowing attached. In 2025/26 the council set a £46.1m programme and delivered £34.2m of it — a £12.0m underspend, with borrowing coming in at £5.3m against £9.2m budgeted. The plan for next year is three times what was actually delivered last year.

The slippage is why MRP came in at £2.706m against a £3.827m budget, and why the CFR will probably land below the £175.4m the strategy forecast. It is a saving that repeats only once: the spend has moved, not gone.

Affordability is moving the wrong way. General Fund financing costs run at 11.60% of net revenue in 2025/26, 12.72% in 2026/27 and 12.93% in 2027/28; the HRA ratio falls slightly, from 7.76% to 7.46%. The out-of-district commercial property portfolio stands at £44.3m, fell 4.2% (£1.95m) in 2024/25, and the June 2026 investment strategy confirms 'a consistent downward movement in capital values across the majority' of it at the 31 March 2026 valuation. That strategy stops new out-of-district acquisitions and commits to disposal after lease re-gearing, with receipts to offset borrowing or be reinvested locally. At outturn the property investments line was £568k over budget.

Two things sit behind all of it. The council repaid its Dexia loan and two PWLB loans in 2025/26, which is why net interest came in £172k under budget — a smaller book, but the LOBO exposure in the maturity chart has not gone. And Ashfield is a Nottinghamshire district inside local government reorganisation: a £566k LGR reserve was created in 2025/26 and £1m of the General Fund surplus transferred into it. The £102.7m programme and the £30.6m of borrowing behind it will be delivered, and repaid, by a successor authority.

officer.subject: Your Cabinet on 21 September — three questions members may put to you
officer.body:
Dear Colleague,

Your Cabinet meets on Monday 21 September. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB rates every working day, and we have been through Ashfield's — the Treasury Management Strategy that went to Council in March, the draft outturn that went to Cabinet in July, and the Corporate Investment Strategy from June.

This is not a criticism of the papers. They are clear and they say what they should. It is the shortlist of questions we would expect a well-briefed member to put to you, sent early enough to be useful rather than after the fact.

What the papers show, in the round. The capital financing requirement is forecast at £175.4m at 31 March 2026 against £82.7m of external borrowing, leaving £92.7m funded internally. Over the same year usable reserves are forecast down from £126.5m to £112.9m and treasury investments from £50.2m to £35.8m. The 2026/27 programme is £102.7m — £58.4m HRA, £44.3m General Fund — carrying a £30.6m borrowing requirement. In 2025/26 the council set a £46.1m programme and delivered £34.2m of it, with borrowing at £5.3m against £9.2m budgeted.

The three we would expect:

1. On the internal borrowing runway. Table 4 holds internal borrowing at roughly £92m out to 2029 while usable reserves fall every year of the same forecast. A member who reads both lines together will ask in which year the cash stops covering the borrowing need, and what rate is assumed when it does. Worth having the answer ready in years, not in principle.

2. On deliverability. The 2026/27 programme is three times what was actually delivered in 2025/26. The obvious follow-up is what changed in delivery capacity — and the sharper one is about the £1.121m MRP underspend, which the outturn attributes to slippage rather than policy. That is a one-off that reverses as the spend lands, and a member who has understood that will want to know how the MTFS treats it.

3. On the commercial portfolio. The investment strategy commits to disposing of the £44.3m out-of-district portfolio after lease re-gearing, having recorded a 4.2% fall in 2024/25 and confirmed further downward movement at the 31 March 2026 valuation. Capital receipts offset the CFR at the price achieved rather than at book value. Expect to be asked how a shortfall between sale proceeds and the debt attributable to an asset would be charged, and over what period. The £568k overspend on the property investments line at outturn will be read alongside it.

On what new borrowing would cost, we can be specific, because we track it daily. The PWLB 10-year maturity rate struck at 6.02% this morning, notice 309/26, with 25-year at 6.65%; the 10-year gilt stands at 4.958%. Your authorised limit for 2026/27 is £201m against a CFR of £175.7m, so the headroom is there — the question members will reach for is what the £30.6m costs at today's rates rather than at the rate the existing book carries.

One observation, offered as such. The February strategy's balance sheet forecast is drawn excluding a planned commercial investment property, while the June investment strategy stops new out-of-district acquisitions. If the forecast still carries an assumption the investment strategy has since dropped, that is worth reconciling before it is quoted back at you.

Every figure above is from Ashfield's own papers or from today's PWLB fixing, and we will send page references for any of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products and we do not advise on borrowing. There is a training library alongside it — short courses on treasury and capital finance, for officers and for members. The ones your papers point to are listed with this email, each with the figure in your own papers that put it there.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org

member.subject: Your Cabinet meets on 21 September — three questions about £30.6m of new borrowing
member.body:
Dear Councillor,

Your Cabinet meets on Monday 21 September. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB borrowing rates every working day, and we have read Ashfield's. This is not a complaint about your council — the papers are clear and the officers have done their job. It is the three questions we would want answered if we were in the room.

First, the position in plain terms. Ashfield has spent £175.4m on capital over the years that it has not yet paid for. It has borrowed £82.7m of that from outside. The remaining £92.7m it has effectively borrowed from itself — using its own cash balances instead of taking a loan. That is a legitimate and, at today's rates, a cheap way to do it. It works only while there is cash to borrow from.

That is the first question, because the cash is falling. Over this year the council's usable reserves are forecast to drop from £126.5m to £112.9m, and its treasury investments from £50.2m to £35.8m. The forecast then holds the £92m of internal borrowing flat out to 2029 while the reserves keep falling. Those two lines converge somewhere. **In which year does the cash stop covering the borrowing, and what borrowing rate is assumed at that point?**

Second, the size of next year's plans. The capital programme for 2026/27 is £102.7m, with £30.6m of new borrowing attached. Last year the council planned £46.1m and actually delivered £34.2m — and borrowed £5.3m rather than the £9.2m budgeted. So next year's plan is around three times what was delivered last year. **What has changed in the council's ability to deliver?** This matters beyond the building work: an underspend is not a saving, it moves the cost into later years, and £1.121m of the reported MRP saving is exactly that.

Third, the commercial property. Ashfield owns £44.3m of investment property outside the district, bought with borrowing. Its value fell 4.2% in 2024/25 and the council's own June strategy confirms values fell again at the March 2026 valuation. The strategy now says the council will stop buying and start selling. The catch is that a sale pays down the debt at the price achieved, not at what the property is in the books for. **If a property sells for less than the borrowing behind it, who pays the difference, and over how many years?**

On what borrowing costs now, we can be precise, because we track it daily. The PWLB 10-year rate for councils struck at 6.02% this morning; the 25-year at 6.65%. That is the price of the £30.6m in the plan, and it is the number worth holding in mind when the programme is presented.

Two further things you may want to note. Ashfield's financing costs — what it pays to service borrowing — take 11.60% of General Fund income this year, rising to 12.72% next year and 12.93% the year after. And all of this sits inside local government reorganisation: the council created a £566k reorganisation reserve last year and moved £1m of its surplus into it. The £30.6m of borrowing agreed now will be repaid by whatever authority replaces this one.

Every figure above comes from Ashfield's own published papers or from today's PWLB rate, and we are happy to send page references for all of them.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products, we do not advise councils on borrowing, and we have no view on what Ashfield should do — which is exactly why we can put the numbers and the questions in front of you and leave the judgement to you. There is also a training library, including short courses written for members rather than accountants. The ones your council's own papers point to are listed with this email, each showing the figure that put it there.

If any of this is useful, or if you want the page references, just reply.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
pwlbtoday.org
